newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling helped by exports, but still weak.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling helped by exports, but still weak.

text.p: Coffee exports helped the Kenyan shilling firm slightly against the dollar on Thursday, but dealers said the currency remains generally soft in the wake of Kenya's major row with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) two weeks ago.
The shilling closed at a commercial mean of 69.97 against the dollar up from 70.17 at open.
"Things were better for the shilling today after we received about $5 million from coffee exporters," a senior dealer from a leading commercial bank told Reuters.

The currency took a beating after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) cancelled the first year of a three-year $205 million aid package to Kenya after a corruption row boiled over on July 31, since when the Kenyan unit has lost about 17 percent against the dollar.
Commercial bank dealers said foreign fears had eased, but the underlying tone still remained weak for the shilling.
"Foreigners are no longer buying aggressively. They've become more tolerant and are quoting slightly lower rates. They've seen there's no need to get burnt," one dealer said.
On Wednesday, the Central Bank of Kenya said the shilling exchange rate would continue to be determined by market forces.
"The central bank will only intervene in the market to smoothen out wild fluctuations in the shilling's exchange rate," the central bank said in a statement.

"Accordingly, after the liberalisation of the foreign exchange market, the bank has at no time had a predetermined or desired exchange rate which we wish to see the shilling remain at. However, we would wish to achieve an exchange rate that is both competitive and relatively stable," the statement said.

"The shilling exchange rate shall continue to be determined by market forces of demand and supply which incorporate non-economic sentiments in line with the prevailing government economic, political, fiscal and monetary policies of the day."

The shilling was further undermined this week after the World Bank said it would not release part of a loan under its Structural Adjustment Credit (SAC) until the Kenyan government addressed the IMF's corruption concerns.
